sections.body_en:
The foundation of the partnership between man and woman was established at the time of creation, as it is said (Bereshit 1:27-28): "And God created man in His image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. And God blessed them, and God said to them: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that creeps on the earth." We learn four central matters from the passage of the creation of man: the first, that man was created in the image of God. The second, that this image of God is revealed through the male and the female together. The third, that they have a destiny to be fruitful and multiply. The fourth, that their role is to lead the world and to care for its existence and its cultivation, as it is said further on (2:15): "And the Lord God took the man and placed him in the Garden of Eden to work it and to guard it." It follows that the complete man is the male and the female together, as the Sages said (Yevamot 63a): "Any man who has no wife is not a man," as it is said (Bereshit 5:2): "Male and female He created them, and blessed them, and called their name Adam on the day they were created."

After the first description of the creation of man in a general way, the Torah went back and explained that at first man was created as a single being, with two faces included in him, a male face and a female face. In this man was different from all the animals, for they were all created from the start as two separate kinds, male and female, and only man was created from the start as a single being in whom the male and female were included. This man in whom the two faces were included is called 'Adam Ha-Rishon', and he was the one commanded to repair the world and guard it – "to work it and to guard it" – and he was the one who gave names to all the creatures. And behold, it became clear to Adam that of all the creatures, only he remained alone without a partner, and great sorrow filled his heart. "And the Lord God said: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper corresponding to him" (Bereshit 2:18). "And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and he slept; and He took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the side that He had taken from the man into a woman, and brought her to the man. And the man said: This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man" (ibid. 2:21-23). And although the Creator intended from the start to separate man into male and female, He waited until he would feel his lack. For so Hashem established at the time of the creation of the world, that man would be a partner in the existence and leading of the world, and according to his arousal from below Hashem would lead His world (Zohar II 265a). Therefore only after man was aroused to feel the sorrow of his loneliness, so to speak Hashem saw that it was not good for him to be alone, separated the woman from him, and thereby they could create a loving and fruitful partnership.

Tzela means side, as in tzela ha-mishkan, which means one of the sides of the Mishkan. If so, when Hashem took "one of his tzela'ot" from the man, the meaning is that He took one of his two sides. For at first the male and female were in their almost complete form, but they were joined entirely back to back, with the male face more prominent (see Eruvin 18a).

Since in their root the male and female are united, once they come of age a will and desire is aroused in them to return and be united, and this is what is said (ibid. 2:24): "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh." This is the deep meaning of the mitzva of ona, according to which the spouses are commanded to gladden each other as far as they are able, and thereby to express the love and the unity between them. This is the challenge facing every young man – to find his partner and choose her – and this is the challenge facing every young woman – to choose her partner – and to marry in holiness according to the law of Moshe and Israel. Thereby they complete themselves and the world, and through this they also merit to fulfil the mitzva of 'be fruitful and multiply' and to be partners with Hashem in the birth of new souls.

Something like the story of Adam Ha-Rishon happens with every couple. In their supernal root their souls are joined, and in the process of their descent into the world the soul of the female was separated from the male. Usually the awareness of their original unity remained more with the male, and therefore usually he is the one who feels a stronger and more outward will to join with his partner; therefore he is the one who seeks the female who was separated from him, in the way that "a man seeks his lost object" (Kiddushin 2b). Therefore the Torah imposed on the man the obligation and responsibility to seek his partner for marriage, and he is the one who must betroth her as a wife and bring her under the ḥuppa, and he must initiate the union with her for the sake of the mitzva of ona and for the sake of the mitzva of 'be fruitful and multiply'. Also in the mitzva itself, he goes out of himself and comes to her, and she opens herself to him and receives him.

Since it is impossible to fulfil the mitzva of marriage, and the mitzvot of ona and 'be fruitful and multiply', without the participation of the woman, all these mitzvot and virtues belong to the male and the female alike. Therefore when the man does not fulfil his obligation and does not ask his partner to marry him, his partner has a mitzva to find the way to join him to her. And likewise after marriage, if the man is lax in initiating their union as the Torah commands, his wife has a mitzva to find the way to bring him to her, until they are joined completely.

From the revealed side, the male is first, leading and guiding, and therefore he is the one who must initiate the relationship. On the other hand, since the male is considered the continuation of Adam Ha-Rishon and the woman of Ḥava, in a certain respect the female is on a higher level. For the material from which man was created is dust from the ground, as it is said (Bereshit 2:7): "And the Lord God formed the man of dust from the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living soul." Whereas the material from which the woman was created is on a higher level, for it was taken from man, as it is said: "And He took one of his sides and closed up the flesh in its place." And He further built the woman in a special way to make her beautiful, as it is said: "And the Lord God built the side that He had taken from the man into a woman" (Eruvin 18a). Therefore the woman has the power to deepen the relationship between them and raise it to a higher level.

The man's power is usually more revealed and outward, and the woman's power is hidden and inward. And since the order of the world is that first the outward side is revealed and afterwards the inward side, at first the man's standing is higher: he seeks his wife and betroths her. But as the years go by, thanks to the woman's virtue, who can receive his initiative and turn it into something complete, her standing in the family rises; to the point that, on a deep look, many times one finds that her influence is greater than the man's.1

notes_en.en: The essential differences between man and woman explained here are expanded further below, 4:9-15, with a description of the mutual relations and the rise of the woman's standing over the course of each couple's married life and over the course of the historical process. Below in chapter 4, notes 4 and 6, there is a reference to those who hold that there are no essential differences between man and woman.

sections.title_en: 3. Emotion and Reason in Choosing a Partner
sections.body_en:
The decision whom to marry is made up of two main parts, reason and emotion. If according to reason alone it is worth marrying, but emotion refuses because it is unable to love the partner, certainly one should not marry. And likewise the reverse: if according to emotion it is worth marrying a certain partner, but reason objects and claims that this relationship will not last, and after a time quarrels and misunderstandings will break out, certainly in such a case too one should not marry. In order to marry, both reason and emotion must agree.

And so we find in the words of the Sages: on the one hand guidance addressed to reason, intended to set criteria for examining and choosing the partner – for example, the guidance to check the character of the bride's brothers, because most children resemble the bride's brothers (Bava Batra 110a), and likewise examining character traits (see Yevamot 79a; Kiddushin 71, and elsewhere), and examining health (Yevamot 64b), and the like. And on the other hand the Gemara establishes (Kiddushin 41a) that even in a place and time where the custom is that parents arrange the matches of their sons and daughters, the groom is obligated to see his partner before the wedding, so that they see whether they will be able to love.

In matters of emotion it is very hard to establish rules; for just as people's faces are different, so their feelings are different, and consequently it is hard to establish guidance in this area. One can nevertheless say that the more a person's character traits are refined, the more he can rely on his feelings; whereas a person with bad traits such as pride, lust and anger is likely to be misled by his feelings in choosing his partner. For example, he will seek a woman of deceptive outward beauty that contradicts her character, or one with whom one can have a good time out but life with her inside the home will be very poor. And likewise a young woman whose traits are bad will prefer an outgoing young man who knows how to make an impression, and perhaps will even manage to become rich, but his traits are not good, and life with him will not be good and joyful.

Also on the rational side of the decision there is no absolute guidance, for people are different and everything depends on character and special talents, and consequently what suits one person does not suit another. But in any case the Sages established several main rules in choosing a partner (as brought in the halakha below), and according to these rules one should decide. And one who tends to hesitate would do well to consult with a wise and experienced person who knows him well.

sections.title_en: 4. Those Who Find It Hard to Decide
sections.body_en:
There are people who by nature find it hard to decide; even buying a garment involves more hesitation for them than is usual, and fateful decisions are very hard for them and cast great fear upon them. And so every time they approach a decision to marry, in order to escape the need to decide, they begin to raise doubts and arguments against, and the fear is so great that the positive feeling towards the partner disappears. This problem grows very much among older single men and women. And the advice for them is to increase the place of reason: as long as according to rational considerations the proposal is good and they are comfortable being with the partner, although emotionally they have doubts, they have a mitzva to marry, and in the course of time they will merit the enormous joy of marriage. And there are those who suffer from severe anxieties, to the point that without calming pills they will not succeed in passing the barrier of the decision to marry; they would prefer to separate, provided they are saved from the suffering of the anxieties. Young men and women who suffer from this have a mitzva to turn to a psychiatrist and take calming pills so that they can marry.2

Question: Must an older young man or young woman compromise? Answer: One can call it compromise. But truly it is not compromise; for when one chooses a good partner there is no compromise in it at all, but on the contrary, a complete life. That is, an enthusiastic young man is not aware that in every choice there is compromise. Perhaps in his mind he knows that there is no perfect person in the world, but in his feeling he senses, rightly, that his life will be perfect. Whereas an older person, who already knows that life is more complex, knows and feels that in every decision there is compromise; and therefore he thinks that life with his partner will not be perfect. But he must know that with all the difficulties, his completeness indeed depends on his marriage. This is the true completeness of a person: that out of his limited reality he progresses and rises. And the more they invest in cultivating the partnership in love and joy, the happier and more complete they will be.

Some think mistakenly that since the Sages said (Sota 2a): "Forty days before the formation of the child, a heavenly voice goes out and says: the daughter of so-and-so for so-and-so," he has nothing to worry about; even if years pass, in the end he will receive his match, and therefore as long as he has not found the perfect young woman for him, even if the young women he has met are very good, he should keep himself for his beautiful and perfect "daughter of so-and-so". But their position is mistaken, and with arguments of so-called 'faith' they harm themselves and neglect the mitzva resting on them to hasten, to choose from among the young women suggested to them the best one for them, and to marry. For free choice is the foundation of man, and the whole Torah is built upon it, in placing on a person the full responsibility for all his deeds. And the Rambam wrote in his responsa (siman 436) that the proof of this is from what is said in the Torah about one who married a woman, that he returns from a voluntary war lest he die in the war and another man marry his wife (Devarim 20:7). And if it was proclaimed from Heaven that his wife would marry so-and-so, then even if he returns from the war he will die in another way and his wife will marry the one proclaimed in Heaven; so what would it help him not to go out to war? Rather one must learn from this that a person's decisions and deeds determine who will be his partner. And so wrote the Tashbetz (2:1), that everything connected with the mitzvot of Hashem, including the mitzva of marriage, is not decreed from Heaven but depends on a person's choice. And the Rambam wrote that wherever words are found in the Sages that seemingly appear to contradict the foundation of free choice, one must understand that their words are not to be taken literally, and their intention is to arouse us to a deep idea that does not contradict free choice.3

notes_en.en: The older a person is, the less enthusiastic he usually is; he is also more aware of the difficulties of life, and therefore he is more afraid to decide on marriage. But many older people do not attribute this to their age; rather it seems to them that they have remained exactly as they were at the age of twenty, and the only reason they are not enthusiastic is that the partner they are meeting is not beautiful and attractive enough. But as the years pass they are less inclined to be enthusiastic and become more choosy. Naturally, as time passes they are suggested older young women, who are considered in their eyes less beautiful. And so they enter a destructive and dangerous spiral. The advice for this is to recognise reality, to know that the enthusiasm they had when they were young will not return. And the choice they must make now should be more rational, measured and deep, with awareness of the difficulties and the shortcomings. This does not mean that they should ignore the question of beauty entirely, but that they should give it lower weight. It is important to emphasise that only in the first stage will older people feel a lack; but in the stages after the wedding there need no longer be a difference between young and older people. For after the wedding love and joy depend on good character traits, on joy of life, on vitality, and on the bond that is woven and deepens between the spouses.

One still needs to interpret the words of the Sages (Sota 2a): "Forty days before the formation of the child, a heavenly voice goes out and says: the daughter of so-and-so for so-and-so." The simple interpretation is that there is indeed one who is the most perfect, and if a person merits to repair himself, he will merit to meet her and choose her. But one who is not repaired may meet her, but because of his blindness he will not see the good virtues in her; something in her appearance will bother him, and so he will lose the best match for him.
One can further interpret that there is not one proclamation in Heaven but thousands of proclamations, from the best match for each person down to the worst. All of them have a common denominator, and therefore they are all suitable to a certain degree, because they all have certain traits and qualities that are needed for his completion; therefore they are all considered "the daughter of so-and-so". If he merits to improve his traits and deeds, he will merit the best. If he goes down a little from his spiritual level, he will merit one a little less good; and if he continues to go down and to delay, he will lose and fall to less good proposals; and if he continues to delay and to go down spiritually, he may end up with the worst possibilities for him. Nevertheless, even if he delayed and lost the good proposals for him and married one of the last possibilities still remaining for him, if he and his wife strive to rise together spiritually and to deepen the bond and love between them, they will merit to uncover inner layers and to climb slowly up the ladder, until through the power of their repentance they can rise from level to level until they become like the best proposal for both of them. For great is the power of choice and repentance to uncover the depths of the soul and to raise a person to the highest heights. And likewise on the other hand, even one who merited from the start to marry the best proposal for him, and therefore from the start it was very easy for them to build their home in love and joy, if they insist on spoiling their marriage, can deteriorate lower and lower.
In addition, the Gemara in tractate Sota 2a says that only for a first match do they proclaim in Heaven, but for those who marry in a second match they do not proclaim in Heaven, and therefore their match is as hard as the splitting of the Sea of Reeds. And according to the Kabbalists, all souls today are reincarnated souls, and they are in the category of a second match for which there is no proclamation in Heaven, and their match is as hard as the splitting of the Sea of Reeds. And one may say that it is possible that in one soul there will be a part in the category of a new soul and a part in the category of a reincarnated soul, and it will have both the aspect of a first match and that of a second match.

sections.title_en: 5. Good Character Traits and a Connection to Torah
sections.body_en:
The Sages said that if there are two families that provoke and quarrel with each other regularly, or a family whose sons are known as insolent and brazen, who quarrel and fight a great deal, it is fitting not to marry into them, and one should even be concerned lest they are not of the seed of Israel (SA EH 2:2). Admittedly, some of the Aḥaronim wrote that as a result of the exile disputes increased in Israel, and one cannot determine absolutely by these signs the national identity of the family (Yam Shel Shlomo, Kiddushin ch. 4, siman 4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 2:15). But in any case it is clear to all that it is preferable to keep away from families with these negative traits.

The Shulḥan Arukh further mentions three traits that the Sages counted as central traits in the character of the children of Israel: compassion, modesty and acts of kindness (Yevamot 79a). These traits should be the central traits according to which one chooses a partner.

It is fitting for parents to strive greatly to marry their daughter to a Torah scholar, and the Sages said (Pesaḥim 49a): "A person should always sell all that he has and marry the daughter of a Torah scholar, and marry his daughter to a Torah scholar." And they explained that the intention is not literal, to sell all one's property, for one must leave property in order to subsist and earn a living; rather the intention is that the father must strive greatly to marry his daughter to a Torah scholar. In recent generations, in which women who study Torah have increased, in many respects even one whose father is not a Torah scholar, if she studies Torah and the Torah guides her life, has the virtue of the daughter of a Torah scholar. Also one who sets times for Torah, and the Torah guides his life, is considered in many respects as a Torah scholar.

On the other hand, marriage with a person whose life is guided by physical lusts does not turn out well. Therefore the Sages warned a person not to marry his daughter to an ignoramus, for whoever "marries his daughter to an ignoramus is as if he binds her and places her before a lion: just as a lion tramples and eats and has no shame, so an ignoramus strikes and has relations and has no shame" (Pesaḥim 49b). That is, like the lion that tramples its prey and begins to eat its flesh while it is still alive, so the ignoramus has relations with his wife to satisfy his lust and does not wait for his wife to take pleasure and rejoice. Similarly, when the bride is not connected to Torah and good character traits, but only lusts guide her life, she uses marriage to advance herself, and does not go deeply into understanding her husband's heart and gladdening him as far as she is able.

Beyond the fact that one who is not connected to the Torah and its guidance may turn out to be insensitive and inconsiderate, through the connection to Torah the spouses will have a spiritual vision of walking in the ways of Hashem; thereby they will merit elevation of spirit, the Shekhina will dwell between them, and they will be able to go on rising in their love and in all the good deeds connected with establishing a family and building the home.

sections.title_en: 6. The Ratio of the Spouses' Ages
sections.body_en:
When the difference between the groom's age and the bride's age is a number of years, this is no obstacle, whether the groom is older or the bride is older. Admittedly, some say that it is desirable that the groom be older than his wife (Shulḥan Ha-Ezer), but against him several great authorities ruled that there is no flaw in a young man marrying a woman a few years older than he. And there were also places where the custom was that the bride was older than the groom. When the difference is greater (about a third of the number of years of the older of them), it is preferable to refrain, but there is no prohibition in it; and if from various aspects they find themselves suited, they need not refrain from marrying (see the book Ha-Nisu'in Ke-Hilkhatam 2:44).

But when the difference is very great, to the point that one is young and the other old, it is forbidden to marry them, as ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (SA EH 2:9): "A young man should not marry an old woman, nor an old man a young girl." Admittedly, the commentators on the Shulḥan Arukh, the Ḥelkat Meḥokek and the Beit Shmuel, wrote that the prohibition is when the parents arrange the match between them and even pressure the young woman or young man to marry; for then it is clear that they are not marrying out of love, and it is likely that their marriage will not turn out well. And there is even a concern that this situation will cause the young bride to be unfaithful under her old husband. But if the bride of her own accord agreed to marry the old man, it is permitted, on condition that true love dwells between them. And several Torah scholars are even known to have been born of such couples.

The author of the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (EH 2:6) further added on this matter that if the young bride wants to marry the old man because of his wealth and not because of love, it is not fitting that they marry, for in the end her soul will grow used to the wealth and she will loathe her husband.

In a case where the groom is young and the bride old, so that she can no longer bear children, the groom is obligated to refrain from marrying her, because the mitzva of being fruitful and multiplying rests on him. There was a case about six hundred and fifty years ago in Algiers: a young man wanted to marry an old woman who had a great deal of money, and the court in that city wanted to prevent him from doing so, because he would not be able to fulfil with her the mitzva of 'be fruitful and multiply', and because they assessed that he did not truly love her, but only because of her wealth wanted to marry her and inherit her money. The young man complained to the non-Jewish ruler of the city against the heads of the community, who were preventing him and his fiancée from marrying and fulfilling their love; and the heads of the community answered that it should not be done in Israel that a young man marry an old woman. It was agreed between the ruler of the city and the heads of the community that they would send the question to the greatest of the sages of the generation, the Rivash, and do as he would rule. The rabbi answered that although by the essential law the court was right, for many generations the custom has been not to compel in matters of matches, because compulsion in this may cause many quarrels (Rivash 15). In practice, in the view of Rabbi Yosef Karo (SA EH 1:3), when possible the court should compel them not to marry. And in the view of the Rema one should follow the Rivash, not to use means of compulsion in such cases but only to try to persuade. And so is the practice in fact.

sections.title_en: 7. Marriage Between Relatives and Members of the Same Community
sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Yerushalmi Kiddushin 4:4): "A person should cleave to his tribe and his family," for when he marries a woman from his family, the love and faithfulness between them is great, and he merits the support of both families. They further said (Yevamot 62b): "…One who marries his sister's daughter… of him Scripture says (Yeshayahu 58:9): Then you shall call and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and He will say: Here I am." Rashi explains that a person has an extra love for his sister, even more than for his brother, and consequently if he marries his sister's daughter he will love her greatly. And likewise they said in the Midrash (Bereshit Rabba 18:4): if a man married a woman from among his relatives, of him Scripture says (Bereshit 2:23): "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh."

And so the Patriarchs did: Avraham Avinu was the uncle of Sara Imeinu, Rivka Imeinu was the cousin of Yitzḥak Avinu, and Raḥel and Leah the Matriarchs were the cousins of Yaakov Avinu.

But medically it is known that from marriages of relatives children with defects may be born, and the closer the relationship, the more the risk grows. Indeed we find that already one of the greatest of the Rishonim, Rabbi Yehuda He-Ḥasid, wrote in his will (warning 22) that a person should not marry his brother's daughter or his sister's daughter; and presumably he understood that there is danger in this, and therefore commanded not to act according to the Sages' recommendation.

Several of the great Aḥaronim explained that at the time when they married a woman for the sake of Heaven there was no room for concern, for the merit of the mitzva helped them; but when they marry not for the sake of Heaven there is room for concern. And when Rabbi Yehuda He-Ḥasid saw that many do not marry for the sake of Heaven, he commanded that one not marry one's relatives (see Tzitz Eliezer 15:44; Nishmat Avraham EH 2:1, n. 3).

And it seems that in the past, when the conditions of life were hard, and a person was more exposed to the dangers of hunger, illness, wars and pogroms, there was enormous value to the cohesion of the extended family, with whose help they coped successfully with the various dangers, and through which they maintained conditions of life that encouraged continuity and stability. Therefore the benefit of marriage between relatives outweighed the risk of the birth of children with defects (who usually died in their first year). But when the conditions of life improved, there was no longer an existential necessity for tight family cohesion, and consequently one must take more into account the genetic danger in marriages of relatives. Therefore it is recommended today that relatives not marry, in order to prevent hereditary diseases.

Question: Is it desirable to be particular to marry a partner from the same community (eda) or not?

Answer: Admittedly, some hold that it is preferable that the groom and bride be of the same community, or at least of communities close to one another in their ways and customs, so that they can get along better. But the truth is that one should not establish rules in this; on the contrary, we find many couples from different communities who get along well, and indeed the certain difference creates interest and variety. Likewise it is said that the children of mixed couples are more successful and healthier, for the more difference and hereditary distance there is between the spouses' genes, the smaller the risk of the birth of sick children. In addition, one of the great challenges of our period is the ingathering of the exiles and the unification of the people after two thousand years of separation and exile, and marriages between members of different communities make the greatest contribution to the ingathering of the exiles. And so wrote Rav Kook ztz"l, that the forgetting of the lineage of the tribes, although there is mixing and lack in it, also contains a preparation for the unity of the nation, which is the foundation of the redemption and salvation of Israel; and out of the light of the redemption the power of each tribe will be revealed according to its nature, without any harm to unity (see Orot, p. 43).

But on the other hand, when the distance in way of life is too great, difficulties and misunderstandings may arise. Something that should have been self-evident or understood at a slight hint is not taken in at all by the partner.

To sum up, one must weigh every proposal seriously, without taking the community issue into account; only when the mental gaps are too great is there room to examine with more attention whether the proposal is suitable. And likewise one who very much wants to keep all the customs of his community, including keeping the accepted foods and ways of life, would do well to seek a wife from among the daughters of his community.

sections.title_en: 8. May the Younger Sister Marry Before the Elder?
sections.body_en:
Many strive not to marry off a younger brother before an older brother, and are especially particular not to marry off a younger sister before an elder sister. Several Rishonim, such as the Rashbam and the Rosh, mentioned this matter in connection with the marriage of the daughters of Tzelofḥad, who were praised for marrying in the order of their ages. But usually this custom is based on the words of Lavan to Yaakov Avinu (Bereshit 29:26): "It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn."

Before we mention some of the details of the custom, it should be emphasised that by law there is no prohibition for the younger to marry before the elder; rather this is a custom of courtesy and proper conduct of the younger siblings towards the older ones.

Also regarding the custom, it is clear that when the younger sister has already reached her time, she should not wait until the elder marries; for delay and lingering of a young woman at the age at which most girls her age marry may cause severe results. Many are the young women who delayed at the decisive age, and afterwards, when they wanted to marry, no longer found a suitable young man (Responsa Maharsham 3:136).

And some hold that this whole custom applies only when grooms have been found for both daughters and they are now about to marry; then the younger should give the right of precedence to the elder, to marry before her. But if a groom has been found for the younger and a groom has not yet been found for the elder, one should not delay the wedding of the younger until after the wedding of the elder (Igrot Moshe EH 2:1).

Marriage must be out of consent to live together all one's life. As ruled in the Shulḥan Arukh (EH 2:10): "A person should not marry a woman with the intention of divorcing her." Of course, if severe and unexpected problems arise it is permitted and even a mitzva to divorce, but from the outset the plan must be for life. But reality is not simple, and cases of divorce and widowhood occur; and then the question is how long one must wait until it is permitted to marry again.

The Sages established that a divorcee may not marry within three months of her divorce, so that if she gives birth it will be possible to distinguish clearly whether the child is the son of the first husband or the second. And the same law applies to a woman who was widowed: she may not marry again as long as three months have not passed. And to prevent any mistake in this matter, the Sages further decreed that even a woman who cannot bear children, such as an old woman or a barren woman, should not marry before three months have passed from the time she was divorced or widowed (SA EH 13:1).

As for the man, after divorce there is no obligation for him to wait until he may marry another woman. But a man whose wife died may not marry another woman until all three pilgrimage festivals have passed over him, so that through the joy of the festivals the pain of the memory of his late wife will fade, and he will be able to open himself emotionally to a new relationship. In practice it follows that a widower must wait at least a little more than half a year until he is permitted to marry again, and sometimes he will need to wait almost a whole year until three festivals have passed over him. In special cases of great need, for example if he has small children whom he cannot manage to care for, he is permitted to marry before then (SA YD 392:1-2).

sections.title_en: 10. Marrying a Divorced Woman or a Divorced Man
sections.body_en:
By law it is permitted to marry a divorced man or a divorced woman, even if they divorced many times; the question is whether it is recommended. We find in the Talmud (Pesaḥim 112a) that Rabbi Akiva instructed his student Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai not to marry a woman divorced in her husband's lifetime. And the author of the Ḥatam Sofer (1:133) wrote that in any case there is no great flaw in this, and Rabbi Akiva's instruction is only because of modesty, and many are accustomed not to be careful about it.

But we learn from Rabbi Akiva's guidance that one should not decide on a wedding with a divorced woman in haste; one should check well her character traits and the reasons that caused the divorce, and examine whether these reasons might cause his own marriage with her too to run aground. And likewise regarding a woman: she should not decide in haste to marry a divorced man, but should examine whether the reasons that led to his divorce might harm the marriage with her and destroy it.

Some of the sages said that although by law it is permitted to marry a widow three months after her husband's death, it is preferable not to marry her, because it is explained in the books of Kabbalah that there may be resentment on the part of the soul of the deceased against the one who marries his widow, and this resentment may cause danger to the groom or to the widow (Responsa Ḥayim She'al 2:19; Maharsham part 2, 141). And there are those who are concerned about this, and if they decide to marry they arrange for them a special tikkun that the Rashash instituted, so that they will be saved from the danger through it (Rav Pe'alim 2, Sod Yesharim 1). And some say that if there is room for concern, it is only within twelve months of his death, but afterwards certainly there is no need for concern (see Nisu'in Ke-Hilkhatam 2:53).

On the other hand, there are great authorities who were not concerned about this at all. And it is related of the Gaon of Vilna that he himself married a widow, the daughter of a Torah scholar. Similarly it is brought in the book Bnei Yissaskhar in the name of the Maggid of Mezritch that not only is there no concern about the widow remarrying, but if the widow is fit to marry, as long as she does not marry there is no elevation for the soul of her late husband. And this is because, so to speak, because of him his widow remains alone and wretched, and the matter is counted against him.

And if the widow has children, then in marrying her one fulfils a doubled and redoubled mitzva. In addition to the very mitzva of marriage, there is in this kindness and charity of the highest level. For the Talmud (Ketubot 50a) brings the verse that says: "Happy are those who keep justice, who do righteousness at all times" (Tehillim 106:3), and the Sages asked: is it possible for a person to do righteousness at all times? If so, who is this happy one who always does righteousness? And Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani answered: this is one who raises an orphan boy or girl in his home and marries them off.

For long periods almost all weddings were arranged with the help of matchmakers, whose role was to get to know the groom and bride and their families, and according to their best judgement to make a match between them. Admittedly, there were always young men and young women who decided to marry through natural acquaintance and meeting, and there were periods in which most did so. The Sages said (Ta'anit 26b) that there were no festive days for Israel like the fifteenth of Av and Yom Ha-Kippurim, on which the daughters of Israel would go out in borrowed white garments and dance in the vineyards, and the young men would come there in order to find their partners. Apparently then too many found their match through matchmaking, but one who did not find through matchmaking, or who wanted to choose for himself, would go to the vineyards on these holy days and find his match there. After the destruction of the Temple this custom lapsed (see PH Yamim Nora'im 6:12).

In any case the role of the matchmakers is extremely important, and as great as the virtue of the mitzva of marriage, so is the virtue of the matchmaker who merits to help young men and young women establish families. Therefore one who is talented at this has a mitzva to engage in matchmaking as far as he is able. And there is in this also cleaving to the attributes of the Holy One, blessed be He, in that he does kindness with the couple. Further, the Sages said that since the creation of the world the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself has been engaged in matchmaking and helping couples find each other (Bereshit Rabba 68:4).

One must pay the matchmaker for the match. And the payment is according to the accepted custom in that place or in that circle in which the match was made. Some are accustomed to pay the matchmaker a certain percentage of the sum of money that the parents allocate to the groom and bride, and some pay a fixed sum for each match. And it is clear that if a match was made in a place where it is customary to pay, even though the matchmaker's fee was not discussed, one is obligated to pay him as is customary. The obligation to pay applies to anyone who made a match, even if by profession he is not a matchmaker, and even if he came to suggest the match on his own initiative, without a request from the family (Responsa Maharash Engel 3:15). And it is commonly said that when difficulties arise in domestic peace or in the birth of children, it is because they did not pay the matchmaker his fee properly. The custom is to pay a matchmaking fee for a match that succeeded, but for a proposal that did not succeed one does not pay a fee for the trouble, not even for the financial expenses the matchmaker incurred (see Ha-Nisu'in Ke-Hilkhatam 4:37, based on the Mordekhai and the Beit Yosef).

There are circles today in which it is not customary to pay for a match, and only when it concerns a professional matchmaker for whom matchmaking is his livelihood, and it was agreed in advance that he would be paid, does one pay. Indeed, in a place where it is not customary to pay, there is no obligation to pay. And one should add that the main matchmaking fee that everyone was accustomed to pay was for the financial agreements between the two families. For a considerable part of the matchmaker's work was to draw up the agreements between the two sides: how much each side would pay, how the wedding would be held, what house the parents would give the couple, and so on. Therefore in those circles in which the matchmaker does not get involved at all in financial matters, there is room to argue that there is no need to pay him (see Nisu'in Ke-Hilkhatam ch. 4).

However, it seems in practice that it is very fitting to pay a decent fee to every matchmaker, because even without going into the financial matters his work is still complicated, requires a large investment of time, and many times is accompanied by humiliations and ingratitude. And if in the past one could argue that since the matchmakers do not deal with the financial agreements their work is easy, in practice there are today not a few people who find it very hard to find their match, and the phenomenon of late singlehood is spreading, for lack of people willing to invest their time in matchmaking. Therefore there is a need to encourage people to engage seriously in matchmaking. And in order that those talented at it invest their time and energy in it, one must pay them generously, a few thousand shekels for each match that succeeds; and thereby they will have the energy to continue in the holy work, while absorbing the disappointments and insults along the way. And since this is so, one should be concerned that one who does not pay generously the fee of one who engages in matchmaking will have difficulties arise in his married life, because he weakens the hands of the matchmakers and exhausts their strength from helping other singles find their match. Admittedly, rabbis who arrange matches for their students do not expect payment, and their reward is that the couple lives a happy life; consequently there is no obligation to pay them, and there is no need to be concerned that if they are not paid difficulties will arise in the couple's life.

One should add that it is not right to pay professional matchmakers a high payment in advance; rather at the time of registration one may pay a hundred shekels or a little more. But if the match succeeds, then it is right to pay a high sum of thousands of shekels, as will be agreed.

It is fitting for members of a community who find that many of their community's young people do not find their match to appoint a suitable person who will engage in matchmaking for the members of the community. And one should know that the matchmaker's work does not end with suggesting matches; rather the main part of his work is in accompanying and advising until the engagement, and sometimes also afterwards.
